description: I am a Software Engineering student passionate about software development, artificial intelligence, and innovative technology. I am interested in building practical solutions that combine technology and scientific research. For this challenge, I want to develop an intelligent astronaut health monitoring system that can analyze health data, track vital signs, identify potential risks, and provide useful insights to support astronaut safety during space missions.
summary:
Crew Care is an AI-first astronaut health intelligence system built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It combines daily crew self-check-ins, deterministic rule-based health assessments, personal baseline and trend analysis, and an optional AI assistant (Nova) to help crew members and mission control monitor health across a mission.

The system provides four fictional crew profiles with 30-day health histories, a voice-guided emergency intake with structured first-aid procedures for 13 space-relevant emergencies (including CPR, decompression sickness, radiation exposure, and SANS), and an AI health Q&A that returns evidence-grounded, structured answers rather than generic advice. Mission Control can monitor all crew members, review alerts, and track trends across the mission.

Built with Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, and an optional OpenAI-compatible AI provider, Crew Care runs fully in demo mode without a database or API key. It addresses the challenge by making astronaut health data easier to understand, acting on, and communicating - especially in the high-stakes, resource-limited environment of deep-space missions far from Earth.
details:
What it does and how it works

CrewCare is a health monitoring and emergency guide for astronauts. Each crew member does a daily check-in: vitals, mood, sleep quality and symptoms. A rules engine checks each check-in against set limits and against the astronaut's own normal range from the last 30 days, and marks it green, amber or red. Nova, the AI assistant, answers health questions with clear, structured answers based on the astronaut's own readings. In an emergency, you can either tap a shortcut or type what happened in plain words - for example "my crewmate collapsed and is not breathing" - and the app works out what kind of emergency it is and shows a numbered first-aid procedure with pace cues and space-specific notes. The quality is the same either way. Nova reads every step out loud using the device's own voice, so your hands stay free.

Benefits

It gives crew members who are not doctors a clear path in a health crisis, with no ground support needed. It spots health trends before they turn into emergencies. It puts all crew health data in one place for Mission Control, with live alerts, so the team does not have to check four separate reports. The check-ins, scoring and emergency steps work without a database or a paid API.

Intended impact

Missions are going farther from Earth — the Moon Gateway, Mars transit — and the radio delay makes real-time help from a ground doctor impossible. CrewCare is built for that gap: a health guide that is always there, talks you through each step by voice, and lets the crew check, act and report without waiting for a doctor on the ground.

Tools and languages used

Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19, TypeScript. Tailwind CSS 4 for styling. PostgreSQL + Prisma ORM v5 for the database (optional — the demo runs without it). Google Gemini for the AI answers (gemini-3.5-flash-lite), with a rule-based fallback that works with no API key. Web Speech API for Nova's voice (the device's own voice, no paid service). Recharts for the charts. Zod for checking the inputs. Hosted on Vercel. Built on Windows 11, VS Code, Node.js 20.

How it is creative

Most health apps assume there is a doctor, a hospital and a phone signal nearby. CrewCare assumes none of those. The emergency system understands plain English and answers with the same structured steps a trained paramedic would follow, changed for a spacecraft — microgravity, closed air, radiation. Nova reads each step out loud so you can keep your hands on the patient. And the baseline system learns each astronaut's own normal range, so it catches a slow decline that would look fine on a standard chart.

Factors we considered

No ground support: everything works without a live link to Earth or a doctor. Non-medical users: the instructions are written for crew members with basic first-aid training, not doctors. Space risks: the procedures account for microgravity (CPR is different without gravity), closed air (toxic air, CO2), radiation, and SANS (the eye problem astronauts get in space). Demo reliability: a judge can try the whole system without setting up a database or an API key. Privacy: health data stays on the device by default, with no tracking and no third-party health service.
